title: Scope and lifetime
learningGoals: know that a block has its own scope

youtube.title: C++ Scope: Local, Global and Block Variables | C++ Programming EP 27
youtube.description: In this episode you will tell local from global variables, know that a block has its own scope and use a static local variable, with Xecxec the crab. 0:00 Intro · 0:15 Scope and lifetime · 1:17 Local and global · 2:19 Where each variable lives · 2:59 Second program · 4:15 Recap · 4:45 Bug of the Day · 5:38 Challenge · 6:04 Next episode

thumbnail.pose: Xecxec next to rooms in a house, each with its own box

scenes.animation: Tomato title card: EP sticker thuds in, title stamps with a whoosh, Xecxec scuttles in and waves; thud, whoosh, claw-click, sting
scenes.narration: Today we ask where a variable lives. Scope decides where you can use a name, and for how long it exists.

scenes.onScreen: "Scope and lifetime": numbered lines (1. A variable lives inside its braces; 2. A global variable lives for the whole program; 3. A static local keeps its value between calls) and an analogy card: rooms in a house: a box in the kitchen is not visible in the bedroom
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: Scope is the part of the program where a name is visible. A variable made inside braces dies at the closing brace. A global variable lives for the whole program. A static local variable stays alive between calls. Think of rooms in a house. A box in the kitchen is not visible from the bedroom. Think of scope as the walls of a room. A name made inside a pair of braces can be used only inside those braces. Global variables are visible everywhere, and that is a danger. Any function can change them, so bugs are hard to trace. Prefer local variables, and pass values with parameters.
points: A variable lives inside its braces
A global variable lives for the whole program
A static local keeps its value between calls

scenes.onScreen: scope.cpp: a global counter and a local variable
scenes.animation: Code types in with key-tick; butter [HL n] highlight sweeps line by line with marker-swipe; explanation card on the right
scenes.narration: [HL 4] Visits lives outside every function, so it is global. It lives for the whole program. [HL 7] Local lives inside enter. It is created at each call. [HL 8] Each call adds one to visits. [HL 13] The first call prints visits one. [HL 14] The second call prints visits two. Local is ten each time, because it is made fresh. [HL 4] This variable is outside every function. All functions in the file can use it. [HL 7] This variable is born each time the function starts, and it dies when the function ends. [HL 8] Because visits is global, the count survives between calls. [HL 9] Compare the two numbers on the output. One grows, and the other stays the same.

scenes.onScreen: memory boxes: a global in the static region and a local on the stack
scenes.animation: Boxes pop in one by one with size and address tags; arrows draw on as the narrator mentions them; regions are labelled; pop per box
scenes.narration: Look at the two regions. Visits lives in the static region. It stays until the program ends. Local lives on the stack. It is made when enter starts, and it is destroyed when enter ends. Notice where each variable lives. The stack is busy and changes with every call. The static region stays the same for the whole run. Your choice of scope decides where the data goes.

scenes.onScreen: counter.cpp: a static local keeps its value between calls
scenes.animation: Second program or a twist on the first; [HL n] and [TRACK name=value] cues drive the variable tracker; output panel fills line by line with a ding per line
scenes.narration: [HL 5] The word static makes ticket live for the whole program. The start value is set only once. [HL 6] Each call adds one. [HL 7] It returns the new ticket. [HL 11] The first call prints one hundred and one. [HL 12] The second prints one hundred and two, and so on. [HL 5] The word static does not change who can see the name. Only the function can see ticket. It changes how long the variable lives. [HL 7] Because the value stays, the next call continues where the last call stopped.

scenes.animation: Dark-blue terminal: the compile command types with key-tick, the run command types, output prints in mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Save the file as counter dot cpp. Compile it with g plus plus. Then run the program. The program prints one hundred and one, one hundred and two, and one hundred and three. Think of a ticket machine at a station. Each press gives the next number.

scenes.animation: Recap lines tick in one by one with a pop; Xecxec nods after each tick
scenes.narration: Let us recap. One. A local variable lives inside its braces. Two. A global variable lives for the whole program. Three. A block has its own scope. Four. A static local keeps its value between calls. Pause the video. Say these ideas out loud, one time, slowly.
points: A local variable lives inside its braces.
A global variable lives for the whole program.
A block has its own scope.
A static local keeps its value between calls.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: Using a variable outside its block
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; wrong code shakes; the g++ error lines appear in tomato; the fix slides in and the terminal turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. Total is made inside the loop, but we print it after the loop. The compiler says total was not declared in this scope. The variable died at the closing brace. Make it before the loop. A name is valid only between its braces. Here, total lives inside the loop, and the loop ends before the print. Move the line that makes total above the loop. Then the variable lives through the whole function.

scenes.onScreen: Why was the local variable sad? It knew that it would be gone at the closing brace.
scenes.animation: Full tomato screen, card flips in with a rimshot, Xecxec snaps his claw
scenes.narration: Why was the local variable sad? It knew that it would be gone at the closing brace.

scenes.animation: Task card pops in; checklist ticks with a pop; Xecxec holds a tiny pen
scenes.narration: Your challenge: Write a function that counts how many times it was called. Use a static local variable. Call it four times. Hint: a static local variable keeps its value, so add one to it each time. Write your answer in the comments.

scenes.animation: Next-episode card slides up with a whoosh; right side stays empty for end-screen elements; sign-off text types in
scenes.narration: Next time: recursion. Keep coding, says Xecxec!

bug.error:
Compiler output (exactly as g++ prints it):

block.cpp:8:13: error: 'total' was not declared in this scope
    8 |     cout << total << endl;
      |             ^~~~~
bug.why: Total dies at the closing brace of the loop. Make it before the loop, so it lives until the end of main.

challenge: Write a function that counts how many times it was called. Use a static local variable. Call it four times. Hint: a static local variable keeps its value, so add one to it each time.
challengeAnswer: Write static int calls equals zero inside the function. Add one on each call, and print it. After four calls it shows four.
